verdict.rationale: Both refactors look behavior-preserving. Reading the diffs, every error kind, error position, empty-bare case and post-error stop matches the original in each version. A also adds 15 characterization tests covering every error variant, empty values, escape-at-end and multibyte offsets, so the next change to the line format is protected. B adds no tests and leaves the equivalence check only in its report. B also committed locally without being asked, and its scanners still repeat the original index-loop style; A's small scanner helpers and its comment explaining `#[inline(always)]` are easier to maintain.
a_issues: `read_field` no longer updates `pos` when only separators remain. This is harmless but a small internal difference from the original.
Performance relies on `#[inline(always)]`, and the report admits word-only lines were sometimes 3–5% slower. Real dumps were not benchmarked.
b_issues: No tests were added. The exhaustive comparison was thrown away, so nothing in the repo protects the refactor or future format changes.
Scanners keep the original manual `i < n` / `b[i]` loop shapes, and `quoted` and `timestamp` both repeat the separator-after check instead of sharing a helper.
Benchmark covered only one synthetic line shape.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors keep the tokens, errors and end-of-stream behaviour the same. B's pure scanner functions returning Result, plus a single `#[cold]` fail point, read more cleanly than A's stateful helpers. B also adds 15 characterization tests that pin every error kind and position, which protects this and future format changes. A leaves no lasting tests and made an unrequested local commit.

The helpers mix scanning with state mutation (`fail`/`emit` inside each scanner), so the scanning logic is less self-contained.
Performance was checked on a single synthetic line shape only.
